chunks.content: Highlight box Key findings • A prognostic nomogram was developed and validated to predict 3-, 6-, and 12-month cancer-specific survival (CSS) in patients with intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma lung metastasis (ICCLM). • The nomogram-based risk score effectively stratified patients into low- and high-risk groups with significantly different survival outcomes. What is known and what is new? • Patients with intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma generally face low survival and high risk of recurrence, with overall survival rates of approximately 30% and 18% at 1 and 5 years, respectively. • This study establishes a population-based prognostic model integrating age, liver metastasis, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy to enable individualized survival prediction in ICCLM patients. In our study, the 1-, 3-and 5-year CSS rates for patients with ICCLM were 23.9%, 3.3% and 0.8%, respectively, with a median CSS of 5 months. What is the implication, and what should change now? • The nomogram provides refined risk stratification beyond conventional staging systems, allowing clinicians to identify patients with relatively favorable versus extremely poor prognosis. • Low-risk patients may be considered for active multimodal treatment strategies, including systemic therapy and selected locoregional approaches. • For high-risk patients with very limited predicted survival, the model may assist in avoiding overtreatment, prioritizing non-surgical management, and facilitating early palliative care planning. Introduction Primary liver cancer (PLC) predominantly comprises three histological subtypes: hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (ICC), and mixed HCC-ICC ( ). ICC is an epithelial malignancy arising from the biliary epithelium, accounting for 10% to 15% of PLC and ranking as the second most common histological subtype after HCC ( , ). In recent years, the incidence and mortality rates of ICC have increased globally ( , ). Unfortunately, the prognosis for ICC patients, whether surgical or non-surgical, remains unsatisfactory ( ). Even post-curative surgery, the 5-year overall survival (OS) fluctuates between 20% and 35%, coupled with a high recurrence rate spanning 40% to 80% ( , ). As the disease progresses, advanced ICC may metastasize to extrahepatic organs, with the lungs being the most common site of distant organ metastasis ( , ). Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma lung metastasis (ICCLM) distinctly differs from other tumors, necessitating its own unique prognostic prediction model. An effective prediction model can assist clinicians in tailoring the optimal treatment strategy for individual patient prognoses. The traditional tumor-node-metastasis (TNM) staging system primarily focuses on tumor size, lymph node metastasis, and distant metastasis, overlooking other patient attributes such as age, gender, and treatment methods ( , ). As a result, the TNM staging system might not be wholly applicable to all ICC patients, especially those in advanced stages with distant metastasis. There is an urgent need for a more precise staging system tailored for ICCLM patients. The nomogram is a practical and ideal visualization tool for predicting and calculating the outcome probabilities for each patient and has been extensively utilized in aiding clinical decisions ( , ). Given the relative rarity of ICCLM patients, we employed the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) database to study a cohort of ICCLM patients from 2010 to 2020. This research aimed to develop a nomogram to predict cancer-specific survival (CSS) rates for these patients, which subsequently underwent both internal and external validation. The findings suggest that this nomogram can offer clinicians enhanced prognostic prediction, risk stratification, and a valuable tool for clinical decision-making. We present this article in accordance with the TRIPOD reporting checklist (available at https://tcr.amegroups.com/article/view/10.21037/tcr-2025-2083/rc ). Methods Patients and data selection Utilizing the SEER*Stat software (version 8.4.2), we extracted clinical-pathological data and prognostic information of ICC patients from the SEER database spanning the years 2010 to 2020. The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and its subsequent amendments. Given that SEER operates as a de-identified public database, there was no requirement for patient informed consent or ethical approval. Our analysis was conducted in strict adherence to the guidelines set by the SEER database. The clinical variables collected encompassed: year of diagnosis, age, sex, race, marital status, histological grade, tumor stage, surgical interventions, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, liver metastasis, bone metastasis, and brain metastasis. The primary endpoint of this study was the CSS, defined as the duration from the date of diagnosis to the date of death attributed to the cancer. Inclusion criteria were as follows: (I) diagnosis year between 2010 and 2020; (II) ICD site code: C22.1; (III) international Classification of Diseases for Oncology, Third Edition (ICD-O-3) code 8160. Exclusion criteria encompassed: (I) patients diagnosed via autopsy or death certificate; (II) patients with missing pivotal clinicopathological data, such as age, sex, race, marital status, histological grade, and tumor stage; (III) unknown information regarding surgical interventions, chemotherapy, or radiotherapy; (IV) undetermined distant metastasis data (bone, brain, liver); (V) ambiguous cause of death; (VI) indeterminate survival duration; (VII) presence of primary tumors in other locations. Inclusion criteria were as follows: (I) diagnosis year between 2010 and 2020; (II) ICD site code: C22.1; (III) international Classification of Diseases for Oncology, Third Edition (ICD-O-3) code 8160. Exclusion criteria encompassed: (I) patients diagnosed via autopsy or death certificate; (II) patients with missing pivotal clinicopathological data, such as age, sex, race, marital status, histological grade, and tumor stage; (III) unknown information regarding surgical interventions, chemotherapy, or radiotherapy; (IV) undetermined distant metastasis data (bone, brain, liver); (V) ambiguous cause of death; (VI) indeterminate survival duration; (VII) presence of primary tumors in other locations. In this study, a total of 620 ICCLM patients were included. Patients diagnosed between 2010 and 2017 were randomly divided into a training cohort (70%) and an internal validation cohort (30%). Patients diagnosed between 2018 and 2020 were defined as the external validation cohort ( ). During follow-up, a total of 537 CSS events were observed in the entire cohort. As the final multivariable Cox regression model included 4 independent predictors, the events per variable (EPV) ratio was 134.3, which supports the robustness of our multivariable analysis. Statistical analysis In this study, we constructed a nomogram using a training cohort (n=274) and subsequently validated the model with both an internal validation cohort (n=118) and an external validation cohort (n=228). Assisted by the X-tile software, we identified 50 and 70 years as the optimal age cut-off points. For prognostic factors, univariate Cox regression analysis was initially employed to screen relevant variables. Subsequently, the variables with P<0.10 were incorporated into a multivariate Cox regression analysis, leading to the identification of independent prognostic factors associated with ICCLM. We constructed the ICCLM prognostic model using the RMS package in R software. Following this, the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve of the nomogram was plotted, and its discriminative ability was evaluated using the area under the curve (AUC). Through ROC curve analysis, the discriminative power of the nomogram was compared with that of other independent risk factors. Additionally, calibration curves and decision curve analysis (DCA) were generated to further assess the model’s performance. Ultimately, based on the median risk score, all patients were stratified into high- and low-risk groups. The predictive value of the nomogram was validated using survival curves and the log-rank test. All statistical analyses were conducted in R software version 4.3.1, with P<0.05 considered statistically significant. Results Characteristics of ICCLM patients From the SEER database, we identified 1,238 patients diagnosed with ICC accompanied by lung metastasis (LM) between 2010 and 2020. After applying the aforementioned exclusion criteria, 618 patients were excluded, resulting in a total of 620 patients included in this study. Of these, 392 patients diagnosed between 2010 and 2017 were randomly allocated into a training cohort (n=274) and an internal validation cohort (n=118) at a 7:3 ratio. Patients diagnosed between 2018 and 2020, totaling 228, were designated as the external validation cohort. The baseline clinical, pathological, and specific characteristics of the training, internal validation, and external validation cohorts are summarized in . Within the training set, age stratification was performed using the X-tile software (version 3.6.1), revealing that 56.6% of patients were in the age range of 50–70 years. The majority of patients were Caucasian and married. In terms of sex distribution, 55.5% were male and 44.5% were female. Regarding tumor characteristics, Grade III tumors accounted for 21.9%, but notably, a significant portion of the data was categorized as “unknown”. The most common T and N stages were T2 (54.4%) and N1 (54.7%), respectively. Among these patients, 42 (15.3%) had bone metastasis, 93 (33.9%) had liver metastasis, and only 1 (0.4%) had brain metastasis. In terms of treatment modalities, the vast majority of patients (98.5%) did not undergo surgical intervention, 174 patients (63.5%) received chemotherapy, and 24 patients (8.8%) underwent radiotherapy. Prognostic factors for ICCLM patients To assess various prognostic factors, we conducted both univariate and multivariate Cox regression analyses ( ). The results from the univariate Cox regression analysis indicated that age, marital status, brain metastasis, liver metastasis, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy were significantly associated with prognosis (P<0.10). However, factors such as sex, race, histological grade, T stage, N stage, and bone metastasis showed no statistically significant correlation with prognosis. The multivariate Cox regression analysis further identified age, liver metastasis, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy as independent prognostic factors for CSS. Prognostic nomogram development and validation We included all independent risk factors and developed nomograms using the RMS package in R software to predict the CSS of ICCLM patients at 3-, 6-, and 12-month ( ). As depicted by the nomogram, chemotherapy statistically emerged as the most significant factor influencing CSS, followed by age, radiotherapy, and liver metastasis. The C-indices for the training cohort, internal validation cohort, and external validation cohort were 0.723 [95% confidence interval (CI): 690–0.756], 0.761 (95% CI: 0.714–0.770), and 0.758 (95% CI: 0.719–0.797), respectively, confirming

age, liver metastasis, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy as independent prognostic factors for CSS. Prognostic nomogram development and validation We included all independent risk factors and developed nomograms using the RMS package in R software to predict the CSS of ICCLM patients at 3-, 6-, and 12-month ( ). As depicted by the nomogram, chemotherapy statistically emerged as the most significant factor influencing CSS, followed by age, radiotherapy, and liver metastasis. The C-indices for the training cohort, internal validation cohort, and external validation cohort were 0.723 [95% confidence interval (CI): 690–0.756], 0.761 (95% CI: 0.714–0.770), and 0.758 (95% CI: 0.719–0.797), respectively, confirming the high predictive accuracy of the prognostic model. Further, we compared the AUC values across different cohorts ( ). For the SEER training cohort, the AUC for predicting 3-, 6-, and 12-month CSS were 0.818 (95% CI: 0.765–0.870), 0.788 (95% CI: 0.735–0.848), and 0.753 (95% CI: 0.699–0.819), respectively. For the internal validation cohort, the AUC for 3-, 6-, and 12-month CSS were 0.846 (95% CI: 0.767–0.917), 0.853 (95% CI: 0.775–0.921), and 0.804 (95% CI: 0.704–0.896), respectively. For the external validation cohort, the AUC for 3-, 6-, and 12-month CSS were 0.852 (95% CI: 0.795–0.925), 0.777 (95% CI: 0.716–0.849), and 0.763 (95% CI: 0.692–0.840), respectively. Compared to predictions based on individual prognostic factors, the nomogram exhibited superior accuracy in predicting CSS at 3-, 6-, and 12-month ( ). Additionally, calibration curves for the 3-, 6-, and 12-month CSS were plotted for each cohort, showcasing a high degree of consistency between the nomogram predictions and actual observations ( ). Lastly, the DCA curves for all three cohorts further underscored the clinical utility of the nomogram ( ). The Nomogram consistently demonstrated a superior net benefit over the “treat none” (illustrated by the blue line) and “treat all” (illustrated by the green line) strategies across most probability thresholds. Establishment of a risk stratification system based on the nomogram model In our study of 620 patients, KM survival analysis revealed survival rates of 23.9%, 3.3%, and 0.8% at 1-, 3-, and 5-year, respectively, with a median CSS of 5 months ( ). Utilizing the Cox proportional hazards model, we calculated scores for each independent prognostic factor, culminating in a composite risk score for each patient. Subsequently, risk stratification was established based on the median composite risk score across the three cohorts. Our findings consistently indicated that patients in the high-risk group exhibited significantly lower CSS than those in the low-risk group across training, internal validation, and external validation cohort ( ). Within the training cohort, the survival rates for the high-risk group at 3-, 6-, and 12-month were 24.0%, 10.6%, and 3.9% respectively, while those for the low-risk group were 78.6%, 78.6%, and 37.0%. Discussion Surgical resection is considered the only potentially curative treatment for ICC patients. Regrettably, due to the insidious and non-specific early symptoms of ICC, the majority of patients are diagnosed at an advanced stage ( ). As a result, the resection rate for ICC remains low, with a poor prognosis, and the OS rates at 1- and 5-year are approximately 30% and 18%, respectively ( , ). In fact, distant metastasis is a hallmark of advanced ICC, indicating a poor prognosis for patients. It is well known that the TNM staging system primarily focuses on tumor size, lymph node metastasis, and distant metastasis, yet it overlooks other pivotal patient characteristics such as age, sex, and treatment modalities ( , ). Hence, the TNM system might not be entirely appropriate for all ICC patients, especially those with distant metastases. Therefore, it becomes imperative to develop a system that can accurately predict the prognosis of ICCLM. Notably, Shi et al. ( ) constructed nomograms to predict the likelihood of lung and bone metastases in ICC patients at diagnosis. However, no study has yet developed a validated prognostic tool tailored to patients who already present with ICCLM. In this study, we analyzed the baseline demographic and clinical characteristics of the patients. To identify independent prognostic factors, we conducted both univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazard regression analyses. The univariate analysis suggested that age, marital status, brain metastasis, liver metastasis, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy are potential prognostic indicators for patients with ICCLM. Upon multivariate analysis, only age, liver metastasis, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy emerged as independent prognostic factors. A nomogram was subsequently constructed based on these four factors. The model was validated using the C-index, ROC curves, calibration curves, and DCA curves demonstrating good accuracy and high reliability. KM survival curves revealed a significant difference in CSS between the low- and high-risk groups, underscoring the practicality of our model. In summary, the nomogram accurately predicts the 3-, 6-, and 12-month CSS for ICCLM patients. KM survival curves revealed a significant difference in CSS between the low- and high-risk groups, underscoring the practicality of our model. In summary, the nomogram accurately predicts the 3-, 6-, and 12-month CSS for ICCLM patients. Through univariate and multivariate analyses, we discerned that several factors significantly influenced CSS, including age, liver metastasis, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy. However, variables such as sex, ethnicity, marital status, Grade stage, T-stage, N-stage, surgical resection, bone metastasis, and brain metastasis were not identified as independent prognostic determinants. It has been reported that the incidence of ICC increases with age, with a median patient age of 62 years ( - ). The prognosis is typically unfavorable when ICC is accompanied by intrahepatic metastasis ( ). Research by Shi et al. ( ) highlighted that intrahepatic metastasis is a primary factor leading to LM in ICC patients. Consistently, our study found that ICC patients with concurrent liver and lung metastases have a poorer prognosis. Radiotherapy and chemotherapy both hold pivotal roles in tumor treatment ( ). Patients with distant metastases are typically recommended for systemic treatments, such as systemic chemotherapy and targeted therapy ( ). Among these, the combined chemotherapy regimen of gemcitabine and cisplatin is considered the most effective first-line treatment strategy for ICC patients with distant metastases ( , , ). Radiotherapy has also been demonstrated to prolong the survival of ICC patients and reduce the risk of death from tumor-related liver failure ( - ). In our study, both chemotherapy and radiotherapy demonstrated a positive correlation with patients’ survival rates. Further, multivariate analysis revealed that chemotherapy significantly contributes to the survival of ICCLM patients. In a retrospective study on ICC with brain metastasis, the median survival time was found to be only 3.7 months, with patients exhibiting advanced T-stage, untreated primary lesions, lack of radiotherapy, and presence of bone metastases showing unfavorable prognoses ( ). Yuan et al. ( ) also highlighted that the TNM stage is an independent risk factor affecting the prognosis of ICC patients. However, it’s imperative to note that our study specifically focuses on stage IV ICCLM patients. Upon analyzing the prognosis of ICCLM patients, we found that Grade stage, T-stage, N-stage, surgical resection, bone metastasis, and brain metastasis did not constitute independent prognostic factors, which was consistent with our previous studies of patients with bone metastases from ICC ( ). In discussing the indications for surgical resection of distant ICC metastases, Yoh et al. ( ) suggested that surgery is a reasonable option for patients with intrahepatic metastasis, vascular invasion, or regional lymph node metastasis, as long as a complete resection is feasible upon gross examination. Yan et al. ( ) found that for patients with isolated liver metastases, surgery at the primary site (P=0.002) and at the metastatic site (P=0.005) both conferred survival benefits. However, for patients with isolated pulmonary metastases, only surgery at the metastatic site showed a survival advantage (P=0.01), while surgery at the primary site did not demonstrate significant benefits. It is worth noting that given the subjects we studied, the number of patients choosing surgery was relatively small. In conclusion, further research is warranted to validate the therapeutic outcomes of surgery in such patients. In many cancers, nomograms have been demonstrated to be more accurate and user-friendly than traditional staging systems ( , ). Our nomogram ultimately incorporates easily obtainable factors (age, liver metastasis, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy), facilitating individualized calculations for ICCLM patients. Notably, the impact of chemotherapy on CSS was the most significant, with patients undergoing chemotherapy exhibiting higher CSS than those not receiving chemotherapy. In assessing the robustness of our model for predicting CSS across various time intervals, the training cohort, internal validation, and external validation cohorts consistently demonstrated satisfactory predictive performance, with AUC values consistently exceeding 0.75. The C-indices for the training, internal validation, and external validation cohorts were 0.723, 0.761, and 0.758, respectively. A higher C-index generally indicates more accurate prognostic predictions ( ). This suggests that our nomogram offers a high degree of authenticity and reliability in predicting CSS in ICCLM patients. DCA is employed to assess the performance of predictive models in clinical decision-making. It provides an intuitive visualization of the net benefit achieved by adopting a predictive model over alternative strategies, such as treating all or not treating any patients, across different probability thresholds ( - ). Leveraging this approach, we utilized DCA to evaluate our nomogram, and the results underscored its superior clinical utility. nomogram offers a high degree of authenticity and reliability in predicting CSS in ICCLM patients. DCA is employed to assess the performance of predictive models in clinical decision-making. It provides an intuitive visualization of the net benefit achieved by adopting a predictive model over alternative strategies, such as treating all or not treating any patients, across different probability thresholds ( - ). Leveraging this approach, we utilized DCA to evaluate our nomogram, and the results underscored its superior clinical utility. Employing KM survival analysis, we determined that the 1-, 3-, and 5-year CSS of the 620 patients included in this study were 23.9%, 3.3%, and 0.8%, respectively, with a median CSS of 5 months. Moreover, a notable difference in CSS between the low- and high-risk groups was observed, further attesting to the reliability and practicality of our model. While our study offers valuable insights, there are several noteworthy limitations. Firstly, the data for this research was solely derived from the SEER database, implying that the findings might not be entirely representative of regions outside the United States, such as Asia, Africa, and South America. Moreover, the SEER database lacks data on certain factors that could be closely associated with prognosis, such as hepatitis B virus (HBV) or hepatitis C virus (HCV) infections, carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (CA19-9) levels, and vascular invasion. Thirdly, our external validation data also originated from the SEER database, which might influence the robustness of the validation. Finally, our study used complete-case analysis, excluding approximately 50% of the initial cohort due to missing T and N staging data—a potential source of selection bias if missingness relates to disease severity or treatment access. Although statistical power was sufficient (EPV >100), generalizability may be limited by this non-random attrition. Conclusions We constructed and validated a line chart for predicting 1-, 6-, and 12-month CSS in ICCLM patients. Our proposed diagram takes into account four independent risk factors: age, liver metastasis, chemotherapy and radiotherapy. After internal and external verification, it shows good accuracy and clinical applicability, which can help clinicians to implement individual clinical decisions. documents.title: Consensus liver transplantation hepatocellular carcinoma extended criteria

chunks.content: Introduction Chronic liver disease (CLD) is the 12th leading cause of mortality in the United States. Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) accounts for the majority of CLD cases in the United States [ ]. Pakistan ranks moderate for hepatitis B and C, which cause more than 75% of liver cirrhosis and hepatocellular cancer in the WHO Eastern Mediterranean Regional Office (EMRO) region [ ]. Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) increases the frequency of cirrhosis and HCCs requiring liver transplantation (LT) [ ]. Before liver transplantation, acute liver failure and cirrhosis were treated by alleviating symptoms. Effective liver transplantation improves life quality and lifespan [ ]. In the previous few years, more than 5000 liver transplants have been performed in Europe, bringing the total to more than 140,000, resulting in a good post-LT survival rate of 80% in one year and 90% in five years [ , ]. Indications for liver transplant in adults include acute liver failure, cirrhosis from chronic liver diseases, metabolic disorders originating from the liver, liver-related malignancies, polycystic liver disease, hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, and erythropoietic porphyria. Cirrhosis from chronic liver disease is the most common reason for liver transplantation [ ]. The transplant evaluation technique focuses on operational risk assessment, medical compliance, and co-morbidities that could affect graft survival and overall survival with immunosuppressive drugs [ ]. Hepatic cirrhosis and its systemic effects almost always need transplantation in chronic liver disease patients [ ]. Screening patients for liver transplant eligibility is the most important stage. Thus, managing waiting list patients is crucial to preventing mortality and sliding off the list, and boosting post-transplant survival [ ]. Intermediate Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) scores and liver cirrhosis patients can wait over a year on the waiting list for transplantation [ ]. Effective selection of patients for liver transplantation in chronic liver illnesses lowered ICU stays to less than 10% [ ]. Vugts et al. concluded in their study seeking eligibility for liver transplantation that among a total of 732 patients with chronic liver failure, only 5% were eligible for liver transplantation [ ]. Chronic liver diseases are responsible for a large portion of the country’s economic burden. Among Asian countries, Pakistan has the greatest frequency of chronic liver disease. The majority of the patients present with complications due to poor compliance with medications, a lack of satisfactory counseling, late presentation at the time of diagnosis, overuse of Hakimi medications, and a lack of expert centers to deal with these cases across the country. In Pakistan, the need for liver transplantation has risen in recent years. As a result, the first step toward liver transplantation and post-transplant surveillance is proper screening for eligible candidates. The study aims to assess the patients with CLD for liver transplantation and to know the frequency of eligible patients. Materials and methods Study design and sample size A cross-sectional study was conducted at the Department of Medicine, Khyber Teaching Hospital, Peshawar, spanning from June 27, 2022, to December 26, 2022. The sample size was determined to be 149 chronic liver disease patients based on a 5% prevalence of eligible candidates for liver transplantation in patients with chronic liver failure. This calculation was done using a 95% confidence interval and a 3.5% margin of error, as per the WHO calculator for sample size determination, where a smaller margin of error necessitates a larger sample size. Sampling technique The sampling technique employed was non-probability consecutive sampling, whereby participants were selected based on their availability and willingness to participate. Inclusion criteria Inclusion criteria include patients diagnosed with chronic liver disease secondary to chronic hepatitis B and C, Wilson disease, autoimmune hepatitis, and hepatocellular carcinoma, regardless of gender, within the age range of 18 to 70 years. Exclusion criteria Exclusion criteria were established to refine the study population and exclude confounding factors. These included patients with malignancies outside the liver, a history of alcoholism spanning at least six months, substance abuse, active infections, disabling psychiatric diseases, poor compliance with medications, prior radiotherapy to the abdomen, lack of family support, and unwillingness to provide informed consent. Data collection Khyber Medical College Peshawar Institutional Research and Ethical Review Board (IREB) issued approval 304/DME/KMC. All patients with chronic liver disease who met the inclusion criteria were evaluated after receiving written consent from College of Physicians and Surgeons Pakistan (CPSP). the inclusion criteria were evaluated after receiving written consent from College of Physicians and Surgeons Pakistan (CPSP). These patients were requested to sign an informed consent form in writing. A detailed medical history was taken from these patients, followed by a physical examination. All willing chronic liver disease patients were evaluated for liver transplantation eligibility. A phlebotomist was called up, and blood was taken for all relevant tests, including biochemical tests like total bilirubin, serum creatinine complete blood count, serum electrolytes, and international normalised ratio (INR). The etiology of the chronic liver disease was identified by serological tests or polymerase chain reaction (PCR). The metabolic screening was done for hemochromatosis and Wilson disease. HCC was diagnosed and staged based on a biopsy and CT scan. These patients were tested for anesthesia fitness as well. On a pre-designed proforma, all demographic information, patients' laboratory investigations, scans, and the findings of numerous tests were recorded. To eliminate any confounding factor or bias from the study, strict exclusion criteria were used. Data analysis Statistical Package for Social Sciences (SPSS) version 22.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA) was used for the analysis of data. The mean and standard deviation were computed for categorical variables like age, disease duration, and MELD scores. Frequency and percentages were calculated for categorical variables such as gender, stage of liver cirrhosis, presence of HCC, and frequency of eligible candidates. The frequency of eligible candidates was stratified based on age, gender, duration of the disease, etiology of the chronic liver disease, and presence of HCC to see the effect modifications. Post-stratification, the chi-square test was applied to keep the p-value ≤0.05 as statistically significant. Results A total of 149 patients were assessed in this study. The mean age of the participants was 46.81±15.7 years. There were 58.4% (87) male and 41.6% (62) female patients. Regarding the stages of liver cirrhosis, 14 (9.4%) have Stage I, 48 (32.2%) have Stage II and Stage III and 39 (26.2%) have Stage IV liver cirrhosis. Twenty-three (15.4%) patients have concurrent HCC. The mean duration of liver cirrhosis was 18.22±11.7 months. The summary of participants’ demographic information is given in Table . The mean MELD score of the patient was 20.71, and 38 (25.5%) patients were eligible for liver transplantation. The results were further analyzed based on age, gender, duration of cirrhosis, etiology, and presence of HCC. No statistically significant difference was noted in the eligibility of liver transplantation based on age groups, duration of disease, etiology of the disease and presence of HCC was noted except in terms of gender. Female patients were more eligible for liver transplantation than males with a p-value of 0.001. The elaborated results are given in Table . Discussion Liver transplantation stands as a vital therapeutic intervention for individuals facing life-threatening liver diseases, including acute liver failure, end-stage chronic liver disease, primary hepatic cancers, and metabolic disorders. Despite an increase in deceased donor numbers, post-transplant outcomes tend to be less favorable with advanced donor age. Notably, liver transplantation has emerged as an effective treatment for HCC, contributing significantly to transplant indications. However, the persistent demand for donor organs exceeds the available supply. Globally, liver transplantation plays a pivotal role in managing end-stage liver disease, ranking second only to kidney transplantation in terms of major organ transplants. In the United States, organ allocation is governed by protocols established by the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS), which rely on scoring systems like MELD [ ]. The demographic profile of our study population reveals insights into the age and gender distribution of patients with CLD in our setting. With a mean age of 46.81 years and a slightly higher representation of male patients (58.7%), our findings align with general trends observed in CLD populations. This distribution reflects the prevalence of liver diseases, which often exhibit a higher incidence in males and are commonly diagnosed in middle-aged individuals [ ]. While our sample may not fully represent the broader CLD population, these demographic characteristics provide a foundation for understanding the epidemiology of liver diseases in our region. The distribution of liver cirrhosis stages within our study population highlights the severity and progression of liver disease among patients enrolled. The most common liver cirrhosis stage was stage II found in 32.2% each. Stage II cirrhosis emerged as the most common stage, suggesting a significant proportion of patients with moderate liver damage. This finding underscores the importance of early detection and intervention to prevent disease progression and associated complications. The coexistence of HCC in 15.4% of patients within our study population underscores the clinical complexity inherent in managing CLD, especially when malignancy coincides with cirrhosis. The presence of HCC poses significant challenges in treatment planning and prognosis assessment, as it necessitates a multidisciplinary approach to address both the underlying liver disease and the associated

cirrhosis stage was stage II found in 32.2% each. Stage II cirrhosis emerged as the most common stage, suggesting a significant proportion of patients with moderate liver damage. This finding underscores the importance of early detection and intervention to prevent disease progression and associated complications. The coexistence of HCC in 15.4% of patients within our study population underscores the clinical complexity inherent in managing CLD, especially when malignancy coincides with cirrhosis. The presence of HCC poses significant challenges in treatment planning and prognosis assessment, as it necessitates a multidisciplinary approach to address both the underlying liver disease and the associated cancer. The mean duration of liver cirrhosis among our study participants was 18.22±11.7 months, reflecting the chronic nature of the disease and its progressive course over time. This duration highlights the importance of early diagnosis and intervention in CLD management to mitigate disease progression and reduce the risk of complications such as decompensation, portal hypertension, and hepatocellular carcinoma development. Additionally, the relatively short mean duration of cirrhosis observed in our study population underscores the need for timely and comprehensive medical care to optimize patient outcomes and prevent disease-related morbidity and mortality. In our study, CLD presented with diverse etiologies, yet a notable majority of patients were afflicted with hepatitis C. This observation aligns with global epidemiological trends, where hepatitis C remains a predominant cause of CLD, particularly in certain regions and demographic groups. The predominance of hepatitis C-related CLD underscores the ongoing burden of this viral infection on liver health and highlights the need for targeted prevention, screening, and treatment efforts to curb its impact. Our study findings are in line with research conducted by Syed et al., which emphasizes that hepatitis C virus remains the predominant cause of chronic liver disease necessitating liver transplantation [ ]. However, the frequency of waiting list/eligible patients for liver transplant varies among different populations depending upon the stage of liver cirrhosis at the time of presentation in the hospital, MELD score, and available resources. Vugts et al. concluded in their study seeking eligibility for liver transplantation that among a total of 732 patients with chronic liver failure, only 5% were eligible for liver transplantation [ ]. In another study, it was found that nonbiliary cirrhosis, particularly alcohol- and hepatitis C virus-related cirrhosis (60%), and tumors, mainly hepatocellular carcinoma (19%), are the most common indications for LT in Spain. Unusual causes of LT include metabolic diseases like Wilson's disease, familial amyloid polyneuropathy and hyperoxaluria type I, polycystic kidney and liver disease, and some tumors (epithelioid hemangioendothelioma and neuroendocrine tumors) [ ]. Evaluating eligibility for liver transplantation using MELD scores indicated that 25.5% of patients fulfilled the criteria for transplantation. A study conducted in the USA revealed a noteworthy increase in liver transplant candidates among adult patients, rising from 9% between 2002 and 2005 to 23% between 2018 and 2020 (trend, p < 0.0001) [ ]. This underscores a substantial rise in eligibility criteria over a decade-long timeframe. The study's reliance on data from a single center may limit the generalizability of its findings to broader populations or regions due to potential variations in patient demographics, healthcare practices, and access to transplantation services. Additionally, a larger sample size would have strengthened the study's reliability and yielded more robust results. Recruitment from a specific healthcare facility may have introduced selection bias, as patients at this center may not fully represent the diverse population of chronic liver disease patients, especially those lacking access to specialized care. Additionally, the study's omission of certain potential confounding variables concerning transplant eligibility might result in biased estimates of association. Specifically, focusing solely on MELD scores as a determinant of transplant candidacy overlooks other relevant factors such as socioeconomic status, patient preferences, and organ availability, thus limiting the study's comprehensiveness. Conclusions A significant number of patients in Pakistan meet the criteria for liver transplantation, which highlights how critical it is to address the organ shortage. As reputable community members, doctors can shape public perceptions and actions around organ donation. Furthermore, structural improvements that facilitate organ donation and transplantation processes must be implemented in concert with legislators, community stakeholders, and healthcare professionals.
